extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and educated readers interested in foundations, probability, numerical analysis, and the philosophy/aesthetics of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpts addressing (a) formal and practical criteria for randomness and pseudorandom number generation (frequency limits, place-selection insensitivity, statistical tests, LCG design, speed-of-convergence considerations) and (b) criteria and components of mathematical aesthetic judgment and the algorithmic vs. dialectic distinction in mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair-coin frequency axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fair coin tossed n times, let H(n) and T(n) be the numbers of heads and tails. H(n) + T(n) = n and in the limit as n → ∞, H(n)/n → 1/2 and T(n)/n → 1/2; these limits define P(H)=1/2 and P(T)=1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational frequency-probability characterization: probabilities are limiting relative frequencies. The text emphasizes that the probability 1/2 is an asymptotic statement (need not hold for finite n) and underlies the abstraction of the fair coin and fair tosser. Practical application requires assuming sufficiently rapid convergence so that real coins can be judged by finite samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insensitivity to place-selection (no successful gambling system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tosses of a fair coin are insensitive to place selection: if a subsequence of tosses is selected according to any rule R that depends on prior history, the limiting frequency of H and T in that subsequence is still 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed as the 'principle of impotence' in physics: one cannot devise a successful gambling system against a fair coin. Examples: selecting odd-indexed tosses, square-indexed tosses, or tosses following runs of four heads still yields 50/50 in the limit. This insensitivity is often axiomatized for randomness; cheating/sleight-of-hand by the tosser is explicitly excluded in the abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Von Mises definition of randomness
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite sequence x1,x2,... is 'random' in von Mises' sense if every infinite subsequence extracted from it by any policy or rule R (depending on prior history up to the selected item) is ϖ-distributed (i.e., every block of length k appears with limiting frequency 1/2^k, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Mises' definition formalizes place-selection insensitivity across all block sizes (ϖ-distribution). However, Doob proved that no sequence satisfies this requirement (logical self-contradiction), so the criterion is too strong as stated. The historical note motivates weakening the demands for practical pseudorandomness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criteria for pseudorandom number generators (RNGs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For computational use one demands sequences that are easily programmed, inexpensive to produce, periodic with a period sufficiently large relative to the required number of randoms, and 'sufficiently crazy' to pass a battery of statistical tests (frequency tests, runs tests, poker hand tests, spectral tests, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends pragmatic design choices: linear congruential generators (LCGs) of the form X_{n+1} = k X_n (mod m) are popular; choose parameters tied to machine word length (e.g., m = 2^b, multiplier k chosen appropriately) so the period is large (on the order of 2^b). Emphasize that these sequences are deterministic and periodic; they are judged by statistical test performance and computational efficiency rather than by metaphysical unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed-of-convergence requirement for applied probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although frequency probability is defined as a limit, applied probability implicitly assumes that convergence to the limiting frequencies is sufficiently fast for finite-sample judgment of real-world coins or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter highlights a paradox: infinite-sequence probabilities depend only on the tail and finite initial segments are irrelevant asymptotically, yet in practice a long finite run (e.g., a million consecutive heads) would lead to the conclusion the coin is loaded. Thus, an additional (unstated in formal theory) criterion for applied work is rapid convergence or practical detectability of deviations from the ideal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical tests for randomness (practical test-suite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Random sequences used in practice should pass a variety of statistical tests: frequency (monobit) tests, runs tests, poker-hand tests, spectral tests, and other statistical examinations of mixing and independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tests are used to detect deficiencies in pseudorandom sequences. The chapter suggests that passing multiple, varied tests is the operational standard for deeming a deterministic sequence 'random enough' for computational tasks. No single test suffices; choose tests relevant to intended application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of mathematical aesthetic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic appeal in mathematics is associated with order, symmetry, limitation, alternation of tension and relief, realization of expectations, surprise at unexpected relationships/unities, sensuous visual pleasure, juxtaposition of simple and complex, harmony, balance, contrast, unity, and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgments are personal, culturally and historically variable, and can be cultivated/transmitted by teachers and tradition. The text warns that increased technical familiarity may transform or lessen the feeling of surprise (and thus change the aesthetic experience), and that attempts to reduce aesthetic qualities to deep psychophysiological or mystical explanations are met with skepticism. Examples: delight at the golden ratio arising in diverse contexts, later subsumed into abstract explanations (eigenvalue theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of 'order out of chaos' as an aesthetic/math criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics prizes the ability to create order out of apparent chaos—extracting structure, invariants, and patterns from disarray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter classifies four transformations (order out of order; chaos out of order; chaos out of chaos; order out of chaos) and highlights 'order out of chaos' as the most prized. Examples demonstrating this value include Pappus' theorem (geometric order), the prime number theorem (statistical order in primes), and polygon midpoint iteration producing ellipse-like figures. This criterion underlies much of mathematical inquiry and aesthetic appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic mathematics: constructive/approximate criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic mathematics emphasizes finding effective procedures (algorithms) that produce approximations or numerical answers; solutions are judged by practical computability, speed (convergence rate), and suitability to available computing resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Babylonian (iterative) algorithm for √2 yields rapid (quadratic) convergence and practical numerical accuracy. The algorithmic viewpoint values being able to 'do' computations even if full dialectical rigor is absent. This mode is essential in applied problems (e.g., putting a man on the moon) and in numerical analysis where algorithm formation and empirical performance matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic (existence/proof-based) mathematics criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic mathematics focuses on rigorous logical proof of existence or properties of mathematical objects independent of constructive procedures (existential proofs, continuity arguments, general theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using continuity to assert existence of a vertical bisector of area without constructing it. The dialectic approach yields conceptual insight and certitude (true/false statements) even when no effective algorithm is provided. It underpins much of modern abstract mathematics; practitioners may prize it for intellectual completeness even when it yields no explicit construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical analysis evaluation checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete numerical analysis of a problem consists of: (1) formation of algorithms; (2) study of convergence including the rate of convergence; (3) comparison of algorithms to judge relative utility; (4) error analysis including truncation and roundoff error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical analysis combines algorithm design with rigorous (or heuristic) error/convergence analysis. Guidance includes consideration of computing hardware/software constraints, provable vs empirical convergence, a priori vs a posteriori bounds, and recognizing and handling blunders (machine faults, programming errors). Practitioners should both produce algorithms and assess their reliability and efficiency under intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for recognizing a 'good' numerical answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Different criteria may be used to judge a computed solution x~ to f(x)=0: small absolute error |x* − x~| versus small residual |f(x~)| ≈ 0, and practical considerations when f is only approximately computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that context dictates which criterion is preferable: sometimes a small residual is adequate; other times numerical proximity to the true root is required. Numerical analysts must be explicit about their acceptance criteria and be aware that different choices can lead to widely differing assessments of the same computed result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation/teaching criteria illustrated by Chinese Remainder Theorem example
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a theorem with a concrete, accessible problem (e.g., find a number less than 60 from remainders modulo 3,4,5), give a constructive recipe (explicit linear combination), then generalize and give an algebraic proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical/example-driven exposition approach used here is a model for effective mathematical pedagogy: start with a simple, engaging puzzle, demonstrate a constructive method, and then indicate the general proof or generalization. This is both pedagogical and algorithmic: it shows how a specific algorithmic solution motivates a general theorem.
